claims.text: Elevated-temperature structural and chemical stability is governed by lattice distortion induced by atomic-size mismatch together with high configurational entropy.
Lattice distortion impedes atomic diffusion and phase segregation.
Doping with a small amount of a high-misfit element will increase lattice distortion.
Local lattice distortion produces associated residual stresses.
Local lattice distortion and residual stresses act as kinetic barriers to atomic diffusion.
Local lattice distortion and residual stresses inhibit phase separation.
Enhanced lattice distortion raises the activation energy for atomic diffusion.
Raising the activation energy for diffusion suppresses phase and elemental segregation at high temperature.
High configurational entropy thermodynamically favors a homogeneous solid solution.
Nanoparticles with increased lattice distortion will undergo less phase separation than the undoped control during equivalent high-temperature exposure.
Minimal XRD peak-position changes can be used as evidence of reduced phase separation in this experiment.
Retention of a uniform STEM-EDS elemental distribution can be used as evidence of reduced elemental segregation.
Nanoparticles with increased lattice distortion will retain catalytic or thermoelectric performance better than the control during prolonged high-temperature exposure.
The undoped near-equiatomic control is expected to exhibit elemental rearrangement or phase separation under the specified thermal treatments.
The proposed stability mechanism is limited to near-equiatomic, multielement nanoparticles with low noble-metal content over 473–1923 K.
Extreme particle-size distributions or external reactive atmospheres may dominate degradation and invalidate the proposed mechanism.
